screens.title: Class Templates
screens.subtitle: Create reusable, type-safe classes that work for any data type

narration.text: In this chapter we're going to make C++ classes generic so the same implementation can hold integers, strings, or custom objects without duplicating code. Class templates let you write one blueprint with type parameters that become concrete types when you instantiate an object. You will see why this matters by building a simple Pair and a Stack, and by learning the required syntax for defining member functions inside and outside the class template. We'll also contrast explicit instantiation with C++17 class template argument deduction so you understand when the compiler can infer types and when you must provide them. Finally, we'll cover a common pitfall: keeping template definitions in. cpp files, which can lead to linker errors, and the practical guideline to keep templates available in headers. By the end you should be able to choose between function templates and class templates, implement a generic container, and diagnose common template errors. Think about your own code: where do you currently copy-paste containers for different types? That duplication is the exact problem templates solve.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Class templates let you write one class blueprint with type parameters so a single implementation supports many concrete types with compile-time type safety.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives map to practical, code-centered skills. First, you'll be able to define and implement basic class templates so you can create generic containers instead of copying code for each type. Second, you'll learn how to declare and define member functions of a class template, including the special syntax required when definitions are placed outside the class body. Third, you will be able to explain the difference between how function templates and class templates are instantiated, and when the compiler can deduce types automatically versus when explicit types are required. Finally, you'll implement simple generic containers such as Pair and Stack, and run basic tests in main to confirm behavior. Each objective pairs a coding task with the reasoning behind it so you not only type correct code but also understand why templates avoid duplication and preserve type safety. As you practice, reflect on the common mistakes described here; finding and fixing those mistakes is core to mastering templates.

screens.title: Why Class Templates?
screens.subtitle: Eliminate duplicate container code while keeping strong typing

narration.text: Start with a clear problem: without templates you often write the same container logic for each type — IntStack, StringStack, EmployeeStack — duplicating code and increasing maintenance. A class template introduces a type parameter, for example template, and that placeholder becomes a concrete type when you instantiate the class. This gives you compile-time type safety: the compiler still checks types, but you write the code once. A concrete example is a Stack. With a class template Stack, the same methods push, pop, top, isEmpty, and size work for integers, strings, or custom objects so long as the type supports the required operations and can be stored in the underlying storage. A common misconception is thinking templates weaken type checking; the opposite is true: templates preserve and often strengthen compile-time checks because the compiler performs instantiation and type validation for the specific T you use. Another subtle point is that templates are not a runtime polymorphism mechanism — they produce distinct types per instantiation, not a single runtime-vtable polymorphic class. As you adopt templates, focus on a clear contract for T (for example being copyable or streamable) and keep definitions visible in headers so instantiation works reliably. What duplicate container in your code could become a single template?

keyIdea.title: Problem → Solution
keyIdea.text: Templates solve code duplication by letting you write one generic class that the compiler instantiates for each required type with full type checking.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Why Class Templates?
Definition & Motivation
Class templates parameterize types so a single implementation supports many concrete types.
  • Templates use placeholders like T that become real types on instantiation.
  • They remove duplicated code such as separate stacks per type while keeping compile-time checks.
  • Templates create distinct types for each parameter instantiation rather than runtime polymorphism.
  • Design your template's requirements on T explicitly in comments or documentation.
Key Takeaway
Use class templates to capture reusable container logic for any stored type without losing type checks.
Common Mistake
Treat templates like runtime polymorphism; they generate separate types at compile time instead.
Concrete example
// A single Stack template serves many types
template <typename T>
class Stack {
  // push, pop, top, isEmpty, size using std::vector<T>
};

// Then in main
Stack<int> intStack;
Stack<std::string> stringStack;
This shows the same Stack implementation works for int and string. The compiler instantiates separate Stack<int> and Stack<std::string> types from one template.

screens.title: Pair Class Template
screens.subtitle: A compact generic container for two values

narration.text: Let's walk through a complete Pair class template example and see how constructors and member functions work. The Pair template takes two type parameters, T1 and T2. Inside the class you store members of those types and provide getters, setters, and a print function. When you write the class inline, definitions are visible at instantiation, so the compiler can generate the right code. Concrete usage shows instantiating Pair, Pair, and Pair. Note how explicit angle-bracket types are required for pre-C++17 compilers. Writing constructors and member functions inside the class body is straightforward, but whenever you move definitions outside the class you must repeat the template prefix and qualify the member with Pair<T1, T2>. A common misconception is that you can omit the template parameters when qualifying outside the body; doing so causes compilation errors because the compiler cannot match the member to the template. The visual code panel shows the declaration and sample uses; practice instantiating Pair with different types and printing results to confirm behavior. Consider whether your types support the operations you call inside print, like streaming to output.

keyIdea.title: Pair example
keyIdea.text: Pair<T1,T2> demonstrates multiple type parameters and straightforward getters, setters, and construction for mixed-type storage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Pair Class Template
Pair<T1,T2> — code
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

template <typename T1, typename T2>
class Pair {
private:
    T1 first;
    T2 second;

public:
    Pair(T1 f, T2 s) : first(f), second(s) {}

    T1 getFirst() const { return first; }
    T2 getSecond() const { return second; }

    void setFirst(T1 f) { first = f; }
    void setSecond(T2 s) { second = s; }

    void print() const {
        std::cout << "(" << first << ", " << second << ")" << std::endl;
    }
};
Try instantiating Pair with different combinations. Ensure each type used supports the operations you call, for example printing to standard output in print().
Usage examples
Pair<int,double> p1(10, 20.5); Pair<std::string,char> p2("Hello", 'W'); Pair<int,int> p3(100,200);
  • When used with printable types, print() produces human-readable output.
  • Construction is explicit unless using C++17 CTAD to deduce types.
  • If you move definitions outside the class body remember the template prefix and qualified name.
Key Takeaway
Multiple template parameters let Pair store different types in one concise class template.

screens.title: Defining Member Functions Outside the Class
screens.subtitle: The required template prefix and qualification

narration.text: When you choose to place member function definitions outside a class template body, there are two required pieces of syntax the compiler expects. First, you must repeat the template parameter list with template immediately before the definition. Second, you must fully qualify the function name with the template parameters, for example Pair ::print(). This tells the compiler that the function belongs to a class template instantiation, not a free function. Forgetting either the template prefix or the angle-bracket qualification is a source of compilation errors that confuse many learners. A concrete example: moving print() outside the Pair declaration requires the template line plus the Pair<T1, T2> qualification. Practice by moving one small function out of the class and compiling. If you see errors complaining about unresolved symbols or unknown identifier names, check for the missing template prefix or wrong qualification. A useful misconception check: do not try to write Pair::print() without parameters — the compiler needs the template parameters to match the class template. Ending takeaway: the repetition of template parameters is intentional — it makes template structure explicit to the compiler.

keyIdea.title: Syntax rule
keyIdea.text: Always prefix external member definitions with the template declaration and qualify the function with the class template parameters.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Member Function Syntax
Required pattern
template <typename T1, typename T2>
void Pair<T1, T2>::print() const {
    std::cout << "(" << first << ", " << second << ")" << std::endl;
}
Notice the two pieces: the template prefix and the Pair<T1, T2> qualification. Missing either leads to compiler confusion or errors indicating the function is not a member of a template instantiation.
Explanation bullets
  • The template line introduces the parameter names for this definition.
  • The qualified name Pair<T1, T2>::print ties the definition to the templated class.
  • These repetitions are required because templates are instantiated separately by the compiler.
Pro Tip
When moving functions out, compile early: fix one function at a time to isolate missing prefixes or wrong qualifications.

screens.title: Stack Class Template
screens.subtitle: A robust, generic LIFO container using std::vector

narration.text: Now we will examine a full Stack example built on std::vector as underlying storage. The template supports push, pop, top, isEmpty, and size. Notice how push accepts a const T& to avoid unnecessary copying, and pop returns a T by value after checking isEmpty and popping the vector. The sample code uses standard exceptions to signal erroneous operations, for example throwing std::out_of_range when pop or top is called on an empty stack. This design maintains type safety while delegating storage responsibilities to std::vector, itself a class template. A practical misconception is assuming all types work with push and pop equally; the type T must meet the vector storage requirements — typically being copyable or movable. Also be careful when printing stored values: printing requires operator and Stack and exercise sequences of pushes and pops. The stack code demonstrates how templates compose: a template parameter T is used inside a templated standard container, showing nested templates in practice. Conclude by thinking about exception safety and whether you need to return by value or by reference depending on lifetime expectations. Stack Class Template means use std::vector<t> as storage inside stack<t> and provide clear api methods with exception safety for empty conditions.. In practical terms, a robust, generic lifo container using std::vector. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stack design
keyIdea.text: Use std::vector<T> as storage inside Stack<T> and provide clear API methods with exception safety for empty conditions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Stack Class Template
Stack<T> — code
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <stdexcept>

template <typename T>
class Stack {
private:
    std::vector<T> elements;

public:
    void push(const T& item) { elements.push_back(item); }

    T pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw std::out_of_range("Stack is empty, cannot pop.");
        T top_element = elements.back();
        elements.pop_back();
        return top_element;
    }

    const T& top() const {
        if (isEmpty()) throw std::out_of_range("Stack is empty, no top element.");
        return elements.back();
    }

    bool isEmpty() const { return elements.empty(); }
    size_t size() const { return elements.size(); }
};
This implementation emphasizes correct API behavior and exception handling. Test with primitive and user-defined types to see how requirements on T shape your design.
Usage and notes
  • Push and pop delegate storage to std::vector<T>. Ensure T is copyable or movable.
  • top() returns a const reference to avoid copying; pop() returns a value after removal.
  • Throwing exceptions for empty operations is a clear contract for callers.
Key Takeaway
Compose templates: use std::vector<T> inside Stack<T> to create a flexible container while preserving type requirements.

screens.title: Explicit Instantiation vs CTAD
screens.subtitle: When you must write types and when the compiler can deduce them

narration.text: Class templates are usually instantiated with explicit template arguments, for example Pair p1(10,20.5). This explicit instantiation is unambiguous to the compiler and is required in pre-C++17 code. C++17 introduced Class Template Argument Deduction, or CTAD, which allows the compiler to infer template parameters from constructor arguments in many cases, so Pair p1(10,20.5) becomes valid and deduces Pair. However, deduction is not as general as function template deduction; class templates require constructors and patterns that the compiler can analyze for deduction. A common misconception is assuming deduction always works for classes; it does not for every constructor shape or when constructors are ambiguous. When deduction fails, fall back to explicit angle brackets. Another practical point: function templates often deduce types from call-site arguments more aggressively, while class templates historically required explicit types. When teaching or debugging, try both explicit and deduction forms to see compiler diagnostics. As a takeaway, prefer explicit instantiation in library code where clarity matters, and use CTAD locally for concise code when deduction is unambiguous. Explicit Instantiation vs CTAD means explicit instantiation always works; ctad can be convenient but has rules and limitations — use it where deduction is clear.. In practical terms, when you must write types and when the compiler can deduce them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation choices
keyIdea.text: Explicit instantiation always works; CTAD can be convenient but has rules and limitations — use it where deduction is clear.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Instantiation: explicit vs CTAD
Explicit instantiation
Pair<int,double> p1(10, 20.5);
Stack<std::string> s;
Explicit types are reliable in all standards and are often preferred in headers and library interfaces for clarity.
CTAD (C++17)
Pair p1(10, 20.5); // deduced as Pair<int,double>
Stack s;           // may deduce if constructors allow
Deduction simplifies local code but can fail for ambiguous constructors. Use compiler diagnostics to confirm the deduced types.
When to prefer explicit
Library APIs and code intended for multiple standards should prefer explicit template arguments for clarity and portability.
When CTAD helps
Short, local examples and interactive demos benefit from CTAD to reduce visual clutter when deduction is obvious.

screens.title: Templates and Header Files
screens.subtitle: Why template definitions belong in headers

narration.text: A frequent source of frustration is placing template member definitions in a. cpp file and then observing undefined reference or linker errors when instantiating the template elsewhere. Unlike non-template functions, the compiler must see template definitions at the point of instantiation so it can generate code for the specific types you request. If definitions are hidden in a. cpp file, other translation units that include only the header cannot instantiate the template, and the linker cannot find the generated symbols. The practical and common pattern is to keep the entire template — declarations and definitions — in a header (. h or. hpp). Sometimes teams use an inline implementation file, such as. ipp or. tpp, and include that from the header to separate readability while preserving header visibility. When diagnosing linker errors, look for missing template definitions and check whether definitions were compiled in the same translation unit as the instantiation. A helpful misconception check: this is not a linking bug in the linker — it is a visibility issue at compile/instantiation time. Keep templates header-visible to avoid intermittent build problems.

keyIdea.title: Header visibility
keyIdea.text: Template definitions must be visible at instantiation; keep declarations and definitions in headers or included implementation files to avoid linker errors.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Templates & Headers
Keep template definitions visible
Placing definitions in .cpp hides them from instantiation sites and leads to errors.
Symptom
Linker errors like undefined reference to MyTemplate<int>::method when using the template in another translation unit.
Solution patterns include: put definitions in the header, or include an implementation file from the header (for example MyTemplate.hpp includes MyTemplate.ipp).
Why it matters
Templates are instantiated where used. If the compiler doesn't see the definition at that point, it can't generate the code for the concrete type.
Takeaway: prefer header-only templates or clearly included implementation files for predictable builds.

screens.title: Implementing a Queue<T> — Task Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Use std::vector<T> and implement enqueue, dequeue, front, isEmpty, size

narration.text: This is the hands-on activity: implement a generic Queue using std::vector as storage and test it with at least two types. The starter code provides a Task struct and a main with tests. Begin by declaring template class Queue with a private std::vector container. Implement enqueue(const T& item) to push_back, dequeue() to check isEmpty and remove from the front using erase or by maintaining an index, and front() const to return a const reference to the front element, throwing std::out_of_range if empty. For size() and isEmpty(), forward to the vector. A common performance consideration is that erasing front elements in vector is O(n); for this exercise keep it simple and correct, and note alternative structures like deque if performance matters. Test your queue with Queue and Queue using the provided Task that defines operator<< for easy printing. If you encounter exceptions during dequeue or front, verify your isEmpty checks and exception messages. This exercise reinforces template declaration, method implementation, exception use, and testing with different types. In practical terms, use std::vector<t> and implement enqueue, dequeue, front, isempty, size. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

    std::string description;
    int priority;
    Task(std::string desc, int prio) : description(std::move(desc)), priority(prio) {}
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Task& t) {
        os << "[" << t.description << ", P" << t.priority << "]";
        return os;
    }
};

// TODO: Define the Queue class template here

int main() {
    // Tests in chapter source: use Queue<int> and Queue<Task>

Hints & design notes
  • enqueue: push_back to the vector.
  • dequeue: check isEmpty, remove front element; throw std::out_of_range when empty.
  • front: return const T& to the front element; do not return a reference to a temporary.

screens.title: Common Template Errors and How to Fix Them
screens.subtitle: Missing prefixes, wrong qualifications, and linker symptoms

narration.text: This screen catalogs frequent errors and their fixes. First, forgetting the template<...> prefix when defining a member outside the class yields compilation errors because the compiler doesn't know the template parameters for that definition. Second, failing to qualify the member with the template parameters, for example writing Pair::print instead of Pair<T1,T2>::print, also causes errors. Third, placing template definitions in. cpp files causes linker errors like undefined reference to MyTemplate<int>::method; the root cause is the compiler not seeing the definition at instantiation time. When diagnosing, read the compiler and linker messages: missing symbols usually indicate header visibility problems, while unknown identifiers point to missing template prefixes or misqualified names. Concrete fix steps: add the template prefix, use fully qualified names, and move definitions into headers or include an implementation. ipp file from the header. A misconception to avoid: the linker error is not always a missing library; for templates it's often a missing visible definition. After you apply these fixes, recompile and rerun small tests to confirm correct instantiation and behavior. Common Template Errors and How to Fix Them means read errors carefully: add missing template prefixes, qualify names correctly, and keep definitions in headers to resolve common template issues.. In practical terms, missing prefixes, wrong qualifications, and linker symptoms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting path
keyIdea.text: Read errors carefully: add missing template prefixes, qualify names correctly, and keep definitions in headers to resolve common template issues.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Common Mistakes
Missing template prefix
Always begin external definitions with template <...> or the compiler will reject the member definition.
Wrong qualification
Use Pair<T1,T2>::member rather than Pair::member. The template parameters are required to match the declaration.
Hidden definitions
Definitions in .cpp files often cause undefined references at link time. Keep templates in headers.
Quick Fix
Add template prefix and qualified name, then ensure the definition is included in the header visible at instantiation.
Verification
Recompile a minimal test that instantiates the template to confirm the fix. Linker errors should disappear when definitions are visible.

screens.title: Templates in the Standard Library and Composition
screens.subtitle: How standard containers demonstrate template power

narration.text: The C++ Standard Library provides many examples of templates in practice: std::vector, std::list, std::map, and std::set are all class templates. These classes show how templates scale to complex functionality while retaining type safety. Notice how templates can be nested and composed: a Stack often contains a std::vector, illustrating templates used as components inside other templates. When composing templates, be aware of type requirements — the inner template often imposes constraints on T, such as being copyable or comparable. This is why documentation often describes the expected operations or semantic requirements for template parameters. Another practical point is how templates encourage small, testable pieces: implement a clear contract for your template and test it with primitive types and a small custom type, confirming behavior like copy semantics, exception responses, and printing. Templates power the flexible, high-performance containers you use daily. As a reflective question: which standard container best matches the semantics you need when building a custom template-based container? Templates in the Standard Library and Composition means standard library containers are template examples; composing templates gives powerful, reusable building blocks that require clear parameter contracts.. In practical terms, how standard containers demonstrate template power. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Standard library containers are template examples; composing templates gives powerful, reusable building blocks that require clear parameter contracts.

Composition & real-world use
std::vector<T> and other containers are class templates you can reuse inside your templates.
Example: nested templates

Document what operations T must support: copy, move, compare, or stream for printing.
Testing

Key Takeaway

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas from this chapter. Class templates are blueprints that accept type parameters so one class supports many concrete types with compile-time checks. When defining member functions outside the class body, always repeat the template parameter list and fully qualify the class name with its template arguments. For instantiation, explicit template arguments always work; C++17 CTAD can deduce types in many cases but has limitations. Keep template definitions visible in headers to avoid linker errors; if you separate implementation, include an implementation file from the header. Finally, compose templates with standard containers like std::vector<T> and document the requirements on template parameters so users know which operations T must support. These rules together will let you design safe, reusable generic containers and diagnose common template errors efficiently. Take a moment to reflect: which guideline will you apply first when converting duplicated containers into a template?

keyIdea.title: Essential rules
keyIdea.text: Write header-visible class templates, repeat template prefixes when defining methods outside the class, and prefer explicit instantiation when clarity or older standards demand it.
